narrative:
The model estimated a 63% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, so your admission was denied because the school judged the predicted risk too high. This is not a statement that you cannot succeed; it means the application, as presented, did not show enough evidence to offset that risk.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-position decile, where you were in the second decile compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth. That relatively low standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar-exam failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10, slightly below the accepted average of 3.23, was the next most influential factor, but it worked in the opposite direction, modestly supporting a prediction of passing. Your first-year class-position decile was also in the second decile versus an accepted average near the sixth; this was the third most important factor and again pushed toward failure.

To improve a future application, focus on showing sustained academic improvement and bar-readiness. Meet with admissions to understand whether you can appeal or receive feedback, consider retaking the LSAT if your 28 is below the accepted average of about 37, and build a clear plan for strengthening your academic record. You may also want to seek advising and structured bar-exam preparation before reapplying. If you can document meaningful improvement and a credible plan, a later application may present a stronger case.
